title: Interfaces and polymorphism
objective: Write code against what an object can do (an interface), so new kinds can be added without changing the caller.

sources.title: Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (Addison-Wesley, 1994), chapter 1: "Program to an interface, not an implementation"
Python docs: abc, Abstract Base Classes
Python docs: typing.Protocol (structural subtyping, or static duck typing)

simplifies: Real payment methods also handle failures, refunds that partly succeed, and currencies. Python doesn't require a declared interface: any object with a pay() method works (duck typing); an ABC or a Protocol just makes the contract explicit and checkable.

steps.caption: Checkout handles each payment kind in its own branch, calling a different API for each.
Every new kind means another branch in Checkout, the class that already works.

predict.prompt: The shop adds wallets. What has to change?

options.text: Checkout gets another elif, next to the working card and UPI code
options.explanation: Right. Checkout knows every kind by name, so every new kind edits it.
Checkout still has to learn the word 'wallet' and call it.
Checkout has no branch for wallets yet.

steps.caption: An interface names what every payment method can do: pay(amount). It says nothing about how.
Card and Upi each implement pay() their own way. Checkout only knows the interface.
At run time the call goes to whichever object was passed in. Here it's a Upi…
…which talks to the bank in its own way…

predict.prompt: Next week someone passes a Wallet instead. Which pay() runs?

options.explanation: Right. One call, many forms: that is polymorphism. Checkout's code doesn't change.
That one is abstract: it only names the method.
The call goes to the object actually passed in.

exercise.hint: Which classes have an if/elif that names each payment kind?

options.text: Define a PaymentMethod interface (pay, refund, label); each kind implements it, and callers use only the interface
options.explanation: Right. Callers stop naming kinds, so a new kind is a new class and nothing else.

options.text: Move all the if/elif chains into one big helper
options.explanation: Better than three copies, but the helper still changes for every new kind and keeps growing.

options.text: Store the kind as a number instead of text
options.explanation: The branches stay; only their labels change.

exercise.explain: Checkout, Refunds and Receipts now talk only to PaymentMethod. A Wallet class that implements it plugs in without touching any of them: new behaviour comes from new code, not edits to working code.

quiz.prompt: What does "program to an interface" mean?

options.text: Callers depend on what an object can do (its methods), not on which class it is
options.explanation: Right. Then any class that can do those things fits.

options.text: Every class needs a user interface
options.explanation: "Interface" here means the set of methods others may call.
An ABC is one way to state it; in Python any object with the right methods works.

quiz.prompt: Why is an if/elif on a type name often a design smell?

options.text: Each new type forces an edit to that working code, and the chain tends to be copied elsewhere
options.explanation: Right. Polymorphism moves each branch into the class it's about.
Speed isn't the issue; change is.
It does; the problem is design, not syntax.
